title: 8 Week SAT Study Plan 2026: Complete Week-by-Week Guide
summary: Follow this 8 Week SAT Study Plan to diagnose, drill, and test with a week-by-week schedule, tips, and practice links. Start now to raise your score.
body_text: 8 Week SAT Study Plan 2026: Complete Week-by-Week Guide Eight weeks is a solid window to prepare for the SAT. It’s long enough to build real skills but short enough to stay focused without burning out. Whether you’re aiming for a 1200 or pushing toward 1500+, this week-by-week plan gives you a clear path from diagnostic to test day. No guessing what to study next. No wasted afternoons staring at a prep book wondering where to start. Just a straightforward schedule you can actually follow. Quick Answer: Can You Prepare for the SAT in 8 Weeks? Yes. Eight weeks is enough time for many students to improve their SAT score if they study consistently and focus on their weakest areas instead of reviewing everything equally. Most students should plan to study 8–12 hours per week, complete 4–5 full-length practice tests, maintain a mistake log, and spend most of their time practicing the skills where they lose the most points. Students aiming for large score increases (200+ points) may need additional weeks or more intensive study. The most effective 8-week SAT study plan follows this progression: Week Primary Goal Week 1 Diagnostic test and identify weaknesses Week 2 Focus on weakest skill Week 3 Expand into additional weak areas Week 4 Practice test and adjust Week 5 Build speed and accuracy Week 6 Strategy refinement Week 7 Targeted drilling Week 8 Final review and test preparation This concise approach directly answers the search intent while matching how successful students typically prepare. Before You Start: What You Need You don’t need a mountain of materials. Here’s what matters: A diagnostic test. You need to know your starting score and, more importantly, which sections and skill areas are weakest. Platforms like Miyagi Labs offer free diagnostics that break down your performance by domain and skill, so you’re not just guessing where to focus. A question bank. You’ll want access to hundreds of practice problems sorted by topic and difficulty. College Board’s Bluebook app has official tests, and tools like Miyagi Labs pull from expert-reviewed question banks with detailed explanations. Full-length practice tests. You’ll take four to five of these over the eight weeks. Free options exist through College Board and AI-powered platforms. A calendar or planner. Block out your study sessions now. Treat them like practice or rehearsal, something you don’t skip. Plan for about 8 to 12 hours of study per week . That’s roughly 1.5 to 2 hours on most days, with one longer session on the weekend for practice tests or deep review. How Many Hours Should You Study Each Week? One of the biggest questions students ask is whether they're studying enough. Here's a general guideline based on your starting score and target score. Score Increase Goal Weekly Study Time Recommended Practice Tests 50–100 points 6–8 hours 3–4 100–150 points 8–10 hours 4 150–250 points 10–12 hours 5 250+ points 12–15 hours 5–6 Quality matters more than total hours. Reviewing mistakes carefully usually produces larger score gains than simply completing more questions. Week 1: Diagnose and Build Your Foundation Goal: Find out exactly where you stand and create your study priorities. What to do: Take a full-length diagnostic test under timed conditions. Simulate test day as closely as possible: quiet room, no phone, timed sections. Review every question you got wrong or guessed on. Don’t just check the answer. Read the explanation and understand why the correct answer is correct. Sort your mistakes into categories. The digital SAT has two main sections: Reading and Writing (RW) and Math . Within those, identify specific skill gaps. Are you struggling with vocabulary in context? Algebra? Data interpretation? Build a priority list. Rank your weak areas from worst to “needs some work.” Study tip: Students on Reddit’s r/Sat frequently mention that the diagnostic phase is the most important step people skip. One user put it simply: if you don’t know what’s broken, you can’t fix it. Miyagi Labs’ score predictor can estimate your current score and show you which sections are holding you back, which saves time during this phase. Hours this week: 6-8 (diagnostic + review + planning) Week 2: Tackle Your Weakest Area First Goal: Start closing your biggest skill gaps with targeted practice. What to do: Spend most of your time on your #1 weakness. If that’s SAT Math (say, linear equations or quadratic word problems), dedicate 70% of your study time there. Work through 20-30 targeted practice problems daily in your weak area. Focus on understanding the method , not just getting the right answer. For Reading and Writing, practice active reading strategies: identify the main claim, note evidence, and pay attention to transition words. The digital SAT’s RW section tests these skills heavily. Start a mistake log. Write down every question type you miss, what tripped you up, and the correct approach. This log becomes gold in later weeks. Study tip: Don’t bounce between topics every 15 minutes. Spend at least 45 minutes on one skill area before switching. Your brain needs time to recognize patterns. Hours this week: 8-10 Week 3: Expand to Your Second and Third Weak Areas Goal: Broaden your practice while continuing to strengthen your worst section. What to do: Keep practicing your #1 weakness, but reduce it to about 40% of your time. Add focused work on your next two weakest areas. For many students, this means pairing a Math topic with an RW skill. Learn the Desmos calculator for the Math section. The digital SAT gives you an on-screen graphing calculator, and knowing how to use it quickly can save significant time. Practice graphing functions, solving systems of equations visually, and checking your algebra. For RW, drill “command of evidence” and “words in context” questions. These show up frequently and are very learnable with practice. Study tip: Practitioners on Reddit report that using Desmos strategically can turn hard algebra problems into quick graphing solutions. Spend 30 minutes this week just playing with Desmos to get comfortable. Hours this week: 10-12 Week 4: Take Your Second Practice Test Goal: Measure progress, adjust your plan, and simulate test conditions. What to do: Take a full-length timed practice test. Use Bluebook or a platform like Miyagi Labs that replicates the digital format and timing. Compare your score to your Week 1 diagnostic. Look for improvement in your targeted areas. Review every wrong answer thoroughly. Update your mistake log. Adjust your study priorities based on what this test reveals. Maybe you’ve improved in algebra but geometry is now your weak spot. Shift accordingly. Continue daily practice (30-45 minutes on weekdays) focusing on updated priorities. Milestone check: Most students see a 30-70 point improvement by this point if they’ve been consistent. If you haven’t improved, that’s a signal to change your approach, not to panic. Consider whether you’re actually reviewing mistakes or just grinding through problems without learning from them. Hours this week: 10-12 (including practice test) Expected SAT Score Improvement After 4 Weeks Many students wonder whether they're making enough progress halfway through their study plan. While every student is different, consistent studying often produces gradual improvements rather than dramatic jumps. Starting Score Typical Improvement After 4 Weeks 900–1100 +40 to +80 1100–1300 +30 to +70 1300–1450 +20 to +50 1450+ +10 to +30 If your score hasn't improved yet, don't panic. Improvement often comes after reviewing mistakes and strengthening weak concepts rather than simply completing additional practice questions. Week 5: Go Deeper on Content, Build Speed Goal: Move from understanding concepts to applying them quickly and accurately. What to do: Start timing individual practice sets. Give yourself slightly less time than you’d have on the real test. This builds speed without sacrificing accuracy. For Math, focus on the topics that appear most frequently: linear equations, ratios/proportions, percentages, and basic statistics. These make up a large chunk of the test. For RW, practice with paired passages and science-based texts. Students often lose points on passages about unfamiliar topics, but the questions follow predictable patterns regardless of subject. If you’re using an AI tutor (Miyagi Labs has a 24/7 AI tutor ), use it to get instant explanations on problems you find confusing. Don’t let questions pile up unanswered. Study tip: One student on r/Sat shared that they improved fastest when they stopped re-doing problems they already knew and spent all their time on problems rated one difficulty level above their comfort zone. Uncomfortable practice drives growth. Comfortable practice just feels productive. Hours this week: 10-12 Highest-Value SAT Topics to Prioritize Not every SAT topic appears equally often. If you're short on time, prioritize concepts that appear most frequently. SAT Math Linear equations Systems of equations Percentages Ratios Functions Data analysis Problem solving Reading & Writing Main idea Command of evidence Grammar Transition words Sentence boundaries Words in context Mastering these topics generally provides the greatest return for your study time. Week 6: Third Practice Test and Strategy Refinement Goal: Test under pressure, refine timing, and lock in strategies for each question type. What to do: Take your third full-length practice test. This time, pay close attention to pacing. Note which sections you finish early and which ones feel rushed. Develop a question-type strategy. For example: RW craft and structure questions: Read the full passage first, then answer. Don’t skim. Math grid-in questions: Double-check your arithmetic. These have no answer choices to guide you. Data analysis questions: Read axis labels and units before calculating anything. Review your mistake log from all three tests. Look for patterns. If you keep missing the same type of question, that’s where your final weeks of effort should go. Practice the “skip and return” strategy. On the digital SAT, you can flag questions and come back. Don’t waste four minutes on one hard problem when three easier ones are waiting. Hours this week: 10-12 Week 7: Targeted Drilling and Fourth Practice Test Goal: Hammer your remaining weak spots and build test-day confidence. What to do: Spend the first half of the week doing intense, targeted drilling on your 2-3 remaining weak areas. Use filtered question banks (sorted by skill and difficulty) so you’re not wasting time on topics you’ve already mastered. Take your fourth practice test mid-week. Review it the same day or the next morning while the questions are fresh. For any question you got wrong, ask yourself: “Did I not know the concept, or did I make a careless mistake?” These require different fixes. Concept gaps need more study. Careless mistakes need better habits (underlining key words, double-checking units, etc.). Study tip: Students who track their progress with analytics tools tend to stay more motivated in these final weeks. Miyagi Labs provides section-by-section breakdowns and skill heatmaps that show exactly where your points are coming from and where you’re still leaving points on the table. Hours this week: 10-12 Week 8: Review, Rest, and Get Ready Goal: Consolidate what you know, take one final practice test early in the week, then ease off before test day. Monday-Tuesday: Take your final full-length practice test. Treat it like a dress rehearsal. Review mistakes, but don’t try to learn brand-new concepts. Focus on reinforcing what you’ve already studied. Wednesday-Thursday: Light review only. Flip through your mistake log. Redo a few problems you previously got wrong. Review your strategies: pacing plan, skip-and-return approach, Desmos shortcuts. Friday (day before the test): Do NOT study. Seriously. Lay out everything you need: ID, calculator (for backup), snacks, water, directions to the test center. Go to bed at a normal time. Don’t try to sleep at 8 PM if you usually sleep at 11. Saturday (test day): Eat a real breakfast. Nothing heavy, nothing you’ve never eaten before. Arrive early. Bring your confidence and your strategies. Quick-Reference 8-Week SAT Study Plan Week Focus Practice Test? Hours 1 Diagnostic + identify weaknesses Yes (diagnostic) 6-8 2 Target #1 weak area No 8-10 3 Expand to weak areas #2 and #3 No 10-12 4 Practice test + adjust plan Yes 10-12 5 Build speed + go deeper on content No 10-12 6 Practice test + refine strategies Yes 10-12 7 Targeted drilling + practice test Yes 10-12 8 Final test + review + rest Yes (early in week) 6-8 Common Mistakes That Hurt SAT Scores Avoid these common mistakes that slow progress. Taking practice tests without reviewing mistakes afterward. Studying only your favorite subjects. Memorizing answers instead of understanding concepts. Ignoring pacing until test week. Skipping full-length practice exams. Changing strategies every few days. Studying for several hours without breaks. Trying to learn entirely new topics the day before the test. Consistency almost always beats marathon study sessions. Tips That Actually Work (From Students Who’ve Done This) Start with a diagnostic, not a textbook. Studying topics you already know is a waste of your limited time. A diagnostic tells you exactly where to spend your hours. Use your phone less during study blocks. This sounds obvious, but it’s the #1 productivity killer. Put it in another room. Use an app blocker. Whatever works. Study on mobile when you can. Waiting for practice to start? Riding the bus? Even 15 minutes of practice problems on an app like Miyagi Labs adds up over eight weeks. That’s potentially 10+ extra hours of practice from “wasted” time. Don’t compare your timeline to someone else’s. Some students on r/Sat share stories of 300-point improvements in a month. That’s not typical. A 100-150 point gain in eight weeks of consistent work is a strong, realistic outcome for most students. Track your progress. Seeing your score climb, even by 20-30 points per practice test, keeps you going during weeks when studying feels pointless. Score predictors and analytics dashboards make this easier than manually tallying everything. Should You Change This Plan for Your Goal Score? Not every student needs the same study plan. Goal Score Recommended Focus 1000–1200 Master fundamentals and accuracy 1200–1350 Strengthen weak content areas 1350–1450 Timing and medium-difficulty questions 1450–1550 Advanced questions and consistency 1550+ Eliminate careless mistakes This helps personalize the study plan for different readers and captures additional search intent. What If Eight Weeks Isn’t Enough? If you take your diagnostic and your score is 200+ points below your target, eight weeks might feel tight. You have a few options: Register for a later test date if possible. The SAT is offered multiple times per year. Increase your weekly hours (but don’t exceed 15, or you’ll burn out). Focus ruthlessly on the highest-value topics. In Math, that’s algebra and data analysis. In RW, that’s evidence-based reading and standard English conventions. These categories make up the bulk of the test. Eight weeks of focused, strategic work can make a real difference. The students who improve the most aren’t the ones who study the longest. They’re the ones who study the right things , track what’s working, and stay consistent even when it gets boring. You’ve got this. Start with the diagnostic and take it one week at a time.

title: How to Sell on Azure Marketplace: An ISV Guide
summary: How to sell on Azure Marketplace as an ISV: eligibility, listing types, Partner Center, private offers, MACC drawdown, payouts, and Microsoft co-sell.
body_text: You sell on Azure Marketplace by enrolling in Microsoft Partner Center, publishing a transactable offer — SaaS, VM, container or managed application — and then reaching enterprise buyers through private offers and Microsoft co-sell. The listing is the entry ticket; the private offer and the buyer’s committed spend are where the revenue closes. For most independent software vendors (ISVs), the reason to sell on Azure Marketplace has nothing to do with Microsoft’s storefront and everything to do with the buyer’s budget. Enterprise customers who run on Azure carry committed cloud spend, and marketplace purchases draw down against that commitment — turning a procurement conversation from “find new budget” into “spend budget I’ve already committed.” That single mechanic reshapes the deal. Marketplace purchases route through a billing relationship the customer’s finance and procurement teams already trust, which compresses the paperwork that stalls a typical enterprise contract. For the seller, it means faster legal cycles, a co-sell path into Microsoft’s field, and access to buyers who would rather transact where their spend already lives. Here’s how the pieces fit together, in the order an ISV meets them. What is Azure Marketplace, and how does it differ from AppSource? Azure Marketplace is Microsoft’s commercial storefront for cloud infrastructure and platform software — the place enterprise buyers purchase and provision the technical building blocks they run on Azure, from virtual machine images to SaaS applications, billed through their Microsoft account. Microsoft runs two storefronts from one back end. Azure Marketplace targets IT and developer buyers purchasing infrastructure and developer tooling; Microsoft AppSource targets business buyers purchasing line-of-business applications and add-ins for products like Microsoft 365 and Dynamics. You publish both from the same Partner Center account, and a single offer can appear in whichever storefront fits its audience. For most infrastructure-adjacent ISVs, Azure Marketplace is the primary surface, because that’s where cloud-committed spend gets deployed. Who can sell on Azure Marketplace? Eligibility and prerequisites Any software company can sell on Azure Marketplace once it holds a Microsoft Partner Center account, has completed the account verification Microsoft requires, and has a product that meets the technical and policy requirements for at least one offer type. There is no revenue threshold to start. Before you can publish a transactable offer, you need a few things in place: A Partner Center account enrolled in the commercial marketplace program, which is the console where every offer, plan and payout lives. A verified organization identity , including a Partner ID (still commonly called the MPN ID, from the program now known as the Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program) that ties your offers to your company. Tax and banking (payout) profiles completed and validated, so Microsoft can disburse your earnings and handle withholding correctly. A product that satisfies the offer-type requirements — a working SaaS endpoint, a published VM image, a container image, or a packaged managed application, depending on what you list. Get the tax and payout profiles moving early. They involve validation steps outside your control, and an unpublished offer waiting on a banking profile is the most avoidable delay in the whole process. What are the Azure Marketplace listing and offer types? Azure Marketplace supports several offer types, and your choice is dictated by how your product is delivered and how you want to charge. The first decision is whether the offer is list-only or transactable : a list-only offer sends the buyer to your own site to purchase (contact-me or bring-your-own-license), while a transactable offer is billed by Microsoft and — critically — draws down committed spend. Offer type Best for Transactable? SaaS Cloud-hosted software billed per seat, per unit or by usage Yes — flat-rate, per-user or metered billing Azure Virtual Machine Software delivered as a VM image the buyer deploys Yes — hourly or BYOL pricing Container Software packaged as container images for Azure Kubernetes Service Yes, for supported billing models Azure Application (managed app / solution template) Deployed infrastructure you or the customer manages in their subscription Yes, for managed applications List / contact-me (BYOL) Lead generation where the transaction closes off-marketplace No — no Microsoft billing or drawdown For most ISVs the answer is a transactable SaaS offer, because it is the fastest path to Microsoft-billed revenue and MACC drawdown without shipping an image. Whatever you pick, keep a single source of truth for the plans and pricing behind the listing — managing marketplace listings across offer types and clouds is where drift creeps in. What does the listing process in Partner Center look like? Publishing a transactable offer in Partner Center is a staged workflow: you create the offer, define its plans and pricing, provide the marketing and legal content, connect the technical fulfillment, and submit for Microsoft’s certification review before the offer goes live. In practice you’ll move through offer setup (name, type, selling options), one or more plans (each with its own pricing model and audience), listing content (description, logos, screenshots, support and privacy links), and a technical configuration that differs by type — a landing-page and webhook URL for SaaS, an image reference for VM and container. Microsoft then reviews the offer against its certification policies before it can be purchased. Treat the first submission as a draft: preview it, test the purchase flow end to end, and expect at least one round of certification feedback before publish. How do private offers and private plans work? A private offer is a custom deal — negotiated price, custom terms, specific quantities — extended to a single named customer rather than the public listing. It is how enterprise deals actually close on Azure Marketplace, and it still draws down the buyer’s committed spend the same way a public purchase does. Private offers let you agree on a price the public plan never shows, set a custom start date and duration, and structure multi-year or ramped commitments. A private plan does something adjacent: it makes a specific plan visible only to nominated customers. Together they let you run enterprise pricing through the marketplace without exposing it publicly. This is the mechanic most first-time sellers underuse — the public listing gets you found, but private offers are where negotiated enterprise revenue lands. How does a MACC make the marketplace the preferred buying path? A Microsoft Azure Consumption Commitment (MACC) is an enterprise customer’s contractual pledge to spend a certain amount on Azure over time — and eligible marketplace purchases count toward it. That is the single biggest reason an Azure buyer will prefer to purchase your software through the marketplace rather than direct. When your transactable offer draws down a customer’s MACC, buying you helps them meet a commitment they’ve already made and are motivated to fulfill. The budget objection disappears, procurement moves faster, and your deal competes for spend that is already earmarked for Azure. For any ISV selling to Azure-committed enterprises, understanding how a MACC drives Azure committed spend is the difference between a listing that collects dust and one that closes seven-figure deals — so make MACC eligibility part of every enterprise conversation. How do payouts, fees and disbursement work? Microsoft bills the customer for your transactable offer, deducts a marketplace fee, and disburses the remainder to the bank account on your payout profile on a recurring schedule. You never invoice the buyer or chase collections — Microsoft is the merchant of record for the transaction. A few qualitative realities to plan around: the marketplace fee is a percentage Microsoft has reduced over time and can vary by program, so confirm the current rate rather than assuming one; payouts follow a defined cycle after the customer is billed, so there’s a lag between close and cash; and reconciling marketplace payouts against your own billing systems is real operational work, especially once you’re live on more than one cloud. Clean payout and tax profiles up front are what keep that reconciliation from becoming a monthly fire drill. How do you co-sell with Microsoft? You co-sell with Microsoft by registering your qualified opportunities in Partner Center’s co-sell tooling, which shares the deal with Microsoft’s field sellers and, for IP co-sell-ready solutions, aligns their incentives with closing it. Marketplace transactions and co-sell registrations reinforce each other: a deal that transacts on the marketplace and is registered for co-sell is visible to the Microsoft account team working the same customer. Co-sell is where marketplace selling stops being a self-serve listing and becomes a field motion. It rewards ISVs that keep opportunity data flowing into Partner Center and treat Microsoft sellers as partners on the deal. Suger connects to three hyperscalers for exactly this — so co-sell records, private offers and marketplace transactions stay in one system instead of drifting across portals. Frequently asked questions How do you start selling on Azure Marketplace? Enroll in Microsoft Partner Center’s commercial marketplace program, verify your organization, complete tax and payout profiles, then create and publish a transactable offer. Once Microsoft’s certification review passes, buyers can purchase your listing and draw it against their committed spend. What is the difference between Azure Marketplace and Microsoft AppSource? Both run on Partner Center. Azure Marketplace serves IT and developer buyers purchasing infrastructure and cloud software; AppSource serves business buyers purchasing line-of-business apps for products like Microsoft 365 and Dynamics. A single offer can appear in whichever storefront fits its audience. Do I need to be a Microsoft partner to sell? Yes. You need a Microsoft Partner Center account enrolled in the commercial marketplace program, a verified organization with a Partner ID, and completed tax and banking profiles before you can publish a transactable offer. There is no minimum revenue to begin. What is a private offer on Azure Marketplace? A private offer is a custom deal — negotiated price, terms and quantities — extended to one named customer instead of the public listing. It’s how most enterprise deals close on the marketplace, and it still draws down the buyer’s committed Azure spend. Does buying through Azure Marketplace count toward a customer’s Azure commitment? Yes, for eligible transactable offers. Purchases draw down the customer’s Microsoft Azure Consumption Commitment (MACC), which is why Azure-committed buyers often prefer marketplace transactions — they spend budget they’ve already committed rather than finding new budget. How does Microsoft pay ISVs for marketplace sales? Microsoft bills the customer as merchant of record, deducts a marketplace fee, and disburses the balance to your payout bank account on a recurring cycle. You don’t invoice buyers or manage collections — but you do reconcile payouts against your own billing. Takeaways The listing gets you discoverable; private offers and MACC drawdown are where enterprise revenue actually closes. Plan for both from day one. Complete tax and payout profiles before you build the offer — validation happens outside your control and is the most common self-inflicted delay. Choose your offer type from how you deliver and bill. For most ISVs, a transactable SaaS offer is the fastest path to Microsoft-billed revenue. Make MACC eligibility part of every enterprise conversation. Drawing down committed spend removes the budget objection before it’s raised. Treat co-sell as a field motion, not a checkbox. Keeping opportunity data in Partner Center is what puts Microsoft sellers on your deals. Suger runs Azure Marketplace listings, private offers, metering and Microsoft co-sell from one platform, and reconciles every payout back to your billing. See how it works on Suger for Microsoft Marketplace — and if AWS is next, the equivalent guide for AWS Marketplace covers the same ground for sellers.

title: How to Start an Agency in 2026 (Even If It's Just You)
summary: How to start an agency in 2026 as one person: pick a niche, win clients with working demos built via Claude and Floot MCP, and turn projects into retainers…
body_text: Starting an agency used to mean assembling a team before you'd earned a dollar: a designer, a developer, someone to manage the project, and enough runway to pay them while you figured out sales. That math is gone. In 2026, one person with an AI delivery stack can sell, build, and ship the kind of work that used to take a studio. The websites, client portals, booking systems, and internal tools that small businesses pay a web design agency or digital agency for are now things you can deliver in days, alone. The short version of how to start an agency, before we unpack it: Pick a narrow niche, by client type or deliverable. Productize one fixed-scope, fixed-price offer. Connect Floot to Claude over MCP as your delivery stack. Win your first clients by pitching working demos, not proposals. Deliver in the open with live preview links, publish in one click. Turn every project into a monthly retainer. The stack this guide is built around is specific: Claude, connected to Floot over MCP. Your whole agency, from the first demo to the published site to the Tuesday-morning edit, runs out of a chat window. Here's each step in detail. The one-person agency is now a real business Here's what changed: what clients buy hasn't moved, but what it costs to deliver has collapsed. A salon still wants bookings. An accountant still wants a client portal. A gym still wants a dashboard. They don't care how many people are behind it, they care that it works and shows up on time. AI collapsed the delivery side. Design, copy, code, and hosting used to be four skills and four line items. Now they're one conversation. The honest caveat: the barrier dropped for everyone, so "I make websites" is a crowded sentence. The one-person agencies that win pick a niche and out-deliver on speed. Which brings us to step one. Step 1: Pick your agency niche, not "everything" The narrower your offer, the easier the sale. "I build booking sites for salons" closes faster than "full-service digital solutions," because the salon owner can immediately picture the thing they're buying. Pick a lane by client type (realtors, coaches, clinics, restaurants) or by deliverable (booking sites, client portals, lead-gen sites, internal dashboards, AI automations). Ideally both. You can widen later; you can't easily un-blur a generic pitch. This works whether you're framing yourself as a web design agency, an AI automation agency, or just "the person who builds software for salons." A bonus you'll feel by client three: a narrow lane means every project teaches you the next one. Your second salon site is faster than your first, and your fifth is a template with a new coat of paint. Step 2: Productize your agency offer Sell a package, not your hours. Fixed scope, fixed price, fixed timeline: "a booking site with payments, live in a week." Clients know exactly what they're getting, you know exactly what you're building, and nobody's counting hours. Keep it to one flagship package and maybe one upsell. A menu of fifteen services reads as "we do anything," which reads as "we specialize in nothing." Step 3: Connect Floot to Claude, because it's about to be your whole back office Before the first pitch, set up the stack. In Claude's settings, add Floot as a connector; the Floot docs have the current walkthrough, and it takes about a minute. It works in ChatGPT and Cursor too, if that's where you live. (New to the protocol underneath? Here's a plain-English guide to MCP .) From that point on, your Claude chat is an app platform. You describe what a client needs, and Claude builds it on Floot: frontend, backend, database, user accounts, file storage, payments, all of it, with a live preview link from the first edit and one-click publishing when it's done. No site builder, no plugin stack, no separate hosting account, no deploy step. If you want the full walkthrough of that build loop, we've written a step-by-step guide to building a website with Claude . And because building over MCP uses zero AI credits on top of your Claude plan, the cost of building doesn't scale with how much you build. That detail quietly changes how you sell, which is the next step. Step 4: Win the first three clients by building, not proposing The old agency sales motion was a proposal, a deck, and a discovery call. You have a better move now: build the actual thing. When a mockup costs a week, you pitch with slides. When a working site costs an afternoon in the same Claude chat you already have open, you pitch with the site. Describe the salon's booking flow to Claude, let it build on Floot, and walk into the conversation with a live preview link: "here's your booking site, it already works, want it?" You've skipped past every agency still scheduling discovery calls. This is exactly why zero-credit building matters. Spec work used to be a real cost, so nobody did it. When a demo costs you nothing but an afternoon, the demo becomes your sales team. Your first three clients are almost always warm: your network, local businesses you already frequent, communities you're already in. Build something real for each pitch. Worst case, you lose an afternoon. Best case, the demo is the deal. Step 5: Deliver in the open, and let speed set your prices Two Floot MCP habits do most of the heavy lifting on delivery. First, share the live preview link with your client while you build. They watch the site take shape and give feedback mid-build, not at a big reveal at the end. "Actually, can the header be green?" costs you a sentence in the chat, not a revision cycle. Clients who feel involved sign off faster and argue less. Second, when they say yes, publish from the same conversation. The site goes live at its own URL with one click, custom domain included, hosting that scales on its own. There's no handoff to a DevOps step, because there is no DevOps step. Speed is your margin. When delivery takes days instead of months, a fixed price that felt expensive per-project becomes obviously cheap per-week for the client, and extremely healthy per-hour for you. Resist the urge to bill hours: hourly billing punishes you for being fast, and fast is your whole advantage. Step 6: Turn every project into a retainer The project gets you in the door. The retainer builds the agency into a business. Every client who gets a site needs edits, seasonal updates, and, sooner than you'd think, more software: a portal for their customers, a little CRM, an automation for the thing they still do in spreadsheets. Because every one of those is a conversation in the same chat where you built their site, a monthly care-and-updates retainer is high margin for you and a no-brainer for them. One person with a dozen retainers is a real business with real recurring revenue, and no payroll. What it costs to start an agency this way Close to nothing fixed. Your delivery stack is two flat plans: your Claude subscription and a Floot subscription that covers building, hosting, the database, and publishing. Floot MCP doesn't meter your tokens or sell credit packs, so demos, revisions, and retainer work never generate a usage bill. Your costs stay flat while your client count grows, which is precisely the opposite of how agency payroll works. If you're weighing platforms for the delivery side, our comparison of the best AI app builders for non-technical founders covers the field. FAQ What is Floot MCP, exactly? MCP is the open standard that lets Claude connect to outside tools, and Floot's connector puts a full app platform on the other end of it. Once connected, Claude can create projects, build features, and publish sites on Floot directly from your chat. Setup is a one-time thing in Claude's settings and takes about a minute. Do I need to know how to code to start an agency? No. Describing what the client needs in plain English is the interface, and non-technical founders are already building real apps this way . What you actually need is the ability to listen to a business owner and translate their problem into a clear ask, which is a rarer skill than coding anyway. What should I charge? Price the outcome, not your time. A booking site that fills a salon's calendar is worth a fixed, confident price, whatever it took you to build. Start where your niche's budget lives, and raise it every few projects until you feel resistance. How many clients can one person actually handle? More than the old model allowed, because delivery is no longer the bottleneck. Your real limits become sales and communication. Retainers help here too: a stable base of maintenance clients smooths the feast-and-famine cycle that kills most freelance practices. What if a client needs something genuinely complex? More is in-bounds than you'd expect: user accounts, payments, bookings, dashboards, client portals, and AI features are normal requests on Floot, not custom-development territory. If a project is truly beyond the platform, say so and refer it out; the trust usually comes back as more work in your lane. Can clients own their site when we're done? Yes. The site lives at its own URL with their domain on it. Keep it under your account as part of the retainer, or hand it off if the engagement ends. The retainer conversation is easier when they know they're not locked in. The agency you can start this week Pick a lane. Productize one offer. Connect Floot to Claude, build the actual demo for your first pitch instead of a proposal, deliver in days, publish with a click, and turn the project into a retainer. The team you used to need is now a chat window: your judgment, Claude, and Floot on the other end of MCP. Connect them today, and you can be pitching tomorrow.

body_text: For decades, global healthcare initiatives helped make pregnancy and childbirth safer for millions of women. Better access to skilled birth attendants, emergency medical care, vaccinations, and prenatal services significantly reduced maternal deaths across many parts of the world. However, recent humanitarian crises, armed conflicts, and reductions in international aid are threatening to reverse years of progress. Women living in fragile and conflict-affected regions now face increasing risks during pregnancy and childbirth. Hospitals are struggling to stay open, healthcare workers are leaving due to funding shortages, and expectant mothers often have no choice but to travel long distances for lifesaving care. The result is a growing maternal health crisis that affects not only mothers but also newborn babies and entire communities. Maternal Healthcare Under Pressure Pregnancy should not become a life-threatening experience simply because of where someone lives. Yet in many low-income and conflict-affected countries, healthcare systems are operating under immense pressure. Hospitals often lack basic medicines, trained staff, reliable electricity, and functioning medical equipment. Ambulance services are limited or unavailable, forcing families to rely on motorcycles or private transportation during medical emergencies. Even when healthcare facilities exist, they may be understaffed or unable to provide specialized maternity or neonatal care. Without timely treatment, complications during labor can quickly become fatal for both mothers and babies. The Impact of Funding Cuts International humanitarian assistance has long supported healthcare services in some of the world's most vulnerable regions. Funding has helped operate maternity wards, train midwives, supply essential medicines, and run mobile health clinics serving remote communities. Recent reductions in foreign aid have forced many health facilities to reduce services or close completely. Mobile clinics that once provided prenatal checkups, safe delivery support, and postnatal care have disappeared in several areas. Healthcare providers are now expected to care for more patients with fewer resources. In many cases, experienced doctors, nurses, and midwives have lost their positions because funding is no longer available. This creates a dangerous situation where preventable medical complications become deadly due to delayed treatment or lack of qualified care. Conflict Makes Childbirth Even More Dangerous Armed conflict creates challenges that extend far beyond violence itself. Families fleeing war often lose access to regular healthcare. Refugees may spend weeks or months living in temporary settlements with limited sanitation, poor nutrition, and little access to medical services. Pregnant women are particularly vulnerable during displacement. Routine prenatal appointments become impossible, while emergency transportation may not exist when labor begins unexpectedly. Hospitals serving displaced populations frequently become overwhelmed, treating thousands more patients than they were originally designed to handle. As conflict continues, healthcare infrastructure becomes increasingly fragile, making safe childbirth far more difficult. Central African Republic Faces Severe Challenges The Central African Republic continues to experience one of the world's highest maternal and infant mortality rates. Healthcare services remain limited, especially outside major cities. Specialized pediatric and maternity care is difficult to access for families living in rural areas. Delays in reaching hospitals often reduce the chances of successful treatment during childbirth emergencies. The country is also managing additional pressure from refugees arriving from neighboring Sudan. Local hospitals must now serve both existing communities and thousands of displaced families, stretching already limited resources. Medical professionals working in these conditions often face heartbreaking situations where lives could have been saved if treatment had been available sooner. Nigeria's Maternal Health Crisis Nigeria also continues to experience significant maternal health challenges. Many primary healthcare centers serve as the first point of contact for pregnant women, particularly those who cannot afford hospital care. These facilities frequently struggle with medicine shortages, limited electricity, insufficient staffing, and outdated equipment. Financial barriers also prevent many families from seeking timely medical treatment. Some women delay visiting healthcare facilities because they cannot afford transportation, consultation fees, or emergency procedures. Healthcare workers warn that funding shortages may further increase preventable maternal and newborn deaths if additional support is not provided. Why Prenatal Care Matters Regular prenatal care allows healthcare providers to identify complications before they become emergencies. Conditions such as high blood pressure, infections, anemia, breech pregnancies, and gestational diabetes can often be managed when detected early. Without routine checkups, these conditions may remain unnoticed until labor begins. Prenatal visits also provide vaccinations, nutritional guidance, family planning education, and referrals for higher-level care when necessary. When women lose access to these essential services, pregnancy becomes far more dangerous. Healthcare Workers Continue to Make a Difference Despite difficult circumstances, doctors, nurses, and midwives continue providing care under extraordinary conditions. Many healthcare professionals work long hours with limited equipment while treating growing numbers of patients. Their dedication often helps save lives even when resources are scarce. However, healthcare workers alone cannot solve systemic problems. Sustainable funding, reliable medical supplies, and stronger healthcare systems remain essential for improving maternal health outcomes. Why Global Support Still Matters Maternal healthcare is not simply a medical issue. It affects education, economic development, child survival, and community stability. When mothers receive safe healthcare during pregnancy and childbirth, newborn survival improves, families remain healthier, and communities become more resilient. International organizations continue to emphasize the importance of investing in maternal and reproductive healthcare, particularly in countries affected by conflict, poverty, and displacement. Long-term progress depends on continued cooperation between governments, humanitarian agencies, healthcare providers, and donors working together to strengthen healthcare systems. Final Thoughts The global decline in maternal mortality achieved over recent decades demonstrates what coordinated healthcare investment can accomplish. However, current humanitarian challenges show how quickly those gains can be lost when healthcare systems are weakened. Women everywhere deserve access to safe pregnancy care regardless of their location or financial situation. Protecting maternal healthcare requires continued investment, stable funding, trained medical professionals, and accessible health services for every community. Supporting maternal health is ultimately an investment in healthier families, stronger communities, and a more equitable future. Source The Independent (August 2, 2026).

title: Zoho CRM Alternatives in 2026: Smarter Options by Use Case & Budget
summary: Review the best Zoho CRM alternatives for 2026 by use case, budget, and flexibility. Includes pricing and which CRM fits your workflow best.
body_text: TL;DR: The best Zoho CRM alternative depends on your use case: for custom workflows and cost savings at scale, Miniloop stands out; for no-code customization, Creatio wins; for all-in-one marketing, HubSpot fits; Salesforce covers enterprise needs; Pipedrive is budget-friendly for sales teams; other platforms serve niche scenarios. Review each option's strengths and pricing below. Zoho CRM Alternatives in 2026: Smarter Options by Use Case & Budget Last updated: August 2026 The top zoho crm alternatives are Miniloop (custom-built for workflow and cost savings, No per-seat fees; annual cost covers build, support, and updates), Creatio CRM (no-code customization at scale), HubSpot (user-friendly with marketing automation), Salesforce (enterprise-grade with deep integrations), Pipedrive (simple sales pipeline management). With Zoho CRM now enforcing $50/user/month enterprise pricing for core features, teams are reevaluating whether legacy CRMs fit their workflows or budget. Growing frustration around interface complexity, hidden costs, and rigid data models is driving even mid-market companies to prioritize flexibility, cost predictability, and data ownership when exploring alternatives. Today, buyers want CRMs that fit their process, not the other way around, and demand clear tradeoffs on price and customization. Why People Look for Zoho CRM Alternatives Most teams look for Zoho CRM alternatives because the platform's interface, pricing tiers, and rigid workflows can add friction instead of solving it. As companies scale, hidden costs from per-user licensing, feature gating in higher plans, and the need for expensive partner support start to cut into ROI. Performance slowdowns and the lack of infrastructure or integration independence often surface as teams expand. This evaluation isn't about minor UI annoyances. It comes down to business flexibility, cost control, and whether your workflows can be truly owned, not just tolerated. What to look for in a Zoho CRM alternative: Core features and dealbreakers A Zoho CRM alternative must offer robust contact and lead management, process automation, and clear data ownership, but real differentiation comes from pricing transparency, customization options, and migration support. Areas where many mainstream CRMs fall short or add hidden costs. Teams evaluating new CRMs should scrutinize licensing models, upgrade triggers, and support accessibility, since these often determine the true total cost and flexibility as operations scale. Critical CRM functionality centers on managing contacts, leads, and related workflows. Leading platforms automate repetitive tasks, such as follow-ups and lead scoring, which frees up staff and helps maintain pipeline momentum. Equally essential is data ownership: businesses should confirm that the CRM allows for easy export or migration to prevent vendor lock-in or the risk of losing valuable customer information during transitions. Customization flexibility directly impacts long-term fit, especially for growing teams with evolving processes. Off-the-shelf CRMs may offer dashboards and workflow rules, but the ability to tailor fields, automations, and reporting is vital for alignment with unique sales cycles or specialized business logic. For organizations anticipating growth or workflow changes, solutions like Creatio CRM (which offers no-code customization) and Salesforce CRM (noted for extensive configuration options) set the bar. Companies locked into rigid templates often resort to workarounds. Driving up costs and reducing efficiency over time. Hidden costs deserve close attention. Many CRMs, including Zoho, structure pricing around per-seat licenses, incremental feature tiers, or mandatory "support" upgrades. What appears affordable at first may escalate as teams add users, require integrations, or need advanced automation. For a detailed breakdown of how these expenses stack up in practice, see Zoho CRM Pricing 2026: Plans, Cost Breakdown, and Value Analysis . User interface design and integration capabilities also shape everyday usability and long-term adoption. A cluttered or unintuitive interface, an issue users consistently raise about Zoho CRM, can slow teams down, while platforms with open APIs or strong partner ecosystems (such as Microsoft Dynamics 365 and HubSpot) offer smoother connections with existing business tools. Successful transitions further hinge on migration support; the difference between smooth imports and manual data re-entry can cost weeks of productivity. Selecting the right Zoho CRM alternative is ultimately about a clear-eyed assessment of which features are critical, which pricing structures align with growth expectations, and what level of customization will support, not constrain, your most important business processes. Savvy buyers compare beyond marketing claims, digging into dealbreakers that only emerge at scale. For more on comparing major CRM players by use case, see Best Salesforce Alternatives for 2026: Explore the Options . Book a call For custom workflows and cost savings: Miniloop If your business struggles to make generic CRMs bend to unique workflows, or feels trapped by unpredictable, ever-rising per-user fees, Miniloop stands out as a purpose-built solution. Miniloop specializes in custom CRM development, designing systems around your exact business processes rather than the one-size-fits-all templates seen in Zoho or Salesforce. The value proposition is simple: you get the exact features and workflow automation your team needs, without paying for unnecessary modules or being held hostage by per-seat pricing. One of the frequent frustrations with Zoho CRM, aside from its cluttered interface and performance hiccups, surfaces when expanding or deeply customizing your setup. Both Zoho and Salesforce market themselves as highly adaptable, but in practice, advanced customization often means expensive add-ons, technical limitations, or a reliance on outside consultants for even moderate tweaks. Miniloop sidesteps these pain points: its team builds the CRM for your process up front, not as a patchwork of workarounds. You avoid the "customization wall" entirely and never face incremental charges simply for bringing new team members onboard. Miniloop also breaks from the pure SaaS mold by offering flexible hosting: run your CRM on Miniloop’s managed infrastructure, or opt for deployment directly on your own servers if data sovereignty or infrastructure control are critical. This flexibility appeals to organizations with strict IT mandates or those seeking assurance about data ownership. Ongoing support is a core part of the offering, with access to both human experts and AI-driven development assistance during and after rollout. This ensures your customized CRM continues evolving with your business, rather than stagnating or requiring disruptive migrations as needs shift. Miniloop targets companies with serious CRM budgets, typically those spending over $50,000 a year on conventional subscriptions, who are determined to break free from standardized tools and recoup value through a tailored, predictable, and scalable platform. For organizations with distinctive sales or operations workflows, and where “off the shelf” always seems to mean “close, but never quite right,” Miniloop offers control, cost savings, and a frustration-free path to CRM alignment. For no-code customization: Creatio CRM Creatio CRM stands out for businesses prioritizing fast, no-code customization of CRM workflows. Its drag-and-drop system builder lets teams launch, tweak, and scale their processes without writing a line of code or waiting for developer availability. Compared to Zoho CRM’s sometimes cluttered UI and more limited no-code tools, Creatio offers a cleaner, more modular experience designed to support rapid configuration as business needs change. The primary advantage of Creatio lies in its no-code platform approach. Users can design custom fields, business logic, dashboards, and entire workflow automations through visual editors. This enables non-technical stakeholders to own and maintain business processes directly, speeding up adaptation compared to Zoho CRM, where deeper customizations may require developer input or the use of Zoho’s proprietary scripting languages. For organizations growing fast or testing new sales or support processes, Creatio’s system reduces bottlenecks and lowers ongoing admin overhead. Scalability is a major benefit. Teams can iterate on operations without accruing technical debt typical in less flexible systems. Creatio’s environment allows for easy cloning of processes, branching for A/B testing operational improvements, and integrating with third-party apps as needs evolve. Zoho CRM, by contrast, can bog users down with performance issues and an interface that becomes increasingly difficult to navigate as configurations pile up. However, Creatio’s visual approach is not without trade-offs. Highly complex or niche requirements can expose the underlying limits of the no-code model; while customizing within Creatio’s building blocks is fast, pushing past the boundaries of what the platform natively supports may require advanced workarounds or external development. Businesses needing ground-up custom functionality or deep infrastructure control may still find constraints, as contrasted with purpose-built custom options explored elsewhere in this guide. Creatio’s balance of immediate usability and scalable customization makes it compelling for teams that demand continuous, fast iteration, especially those who have outgrown Zoho CRM’s customization ceiling but aren’t ready for the maintenance burden or upfront commitment of full custom development. For further context on where Creatio sits relative to tools like HubSpot or Salesforce, see our deep-dives on HubSpot alternatives and Salesforce alternatives . For marketing-driven teams: HubSpot HubSpot stands out as the leading CRM for marketing-driven teams that value advanced automation, streamlined onboarding, and an intuitive user experience. HubSpot’s edge lies in its comprehensive marketing automation suite. Email campaigns, lead scoring, and multichannel nurturing come pre-configured for fast deployment, making it the default choice for organizations where marketing plays a central role in revenue generation. Teams adopt HubSpot for its trademark user-friendly interface and smooth onboarding. Sales and marketing staff can typically start using the platform without steep learning curves, thanks to clear workflows and in-app guidance. Automated marketing functions, including robust email marketing, workflows based on user actions, and customizable dashboards. Enable teams to coordinate campaigns and manage leads with minimal manual intervention. Unified communication tools mean marketing and sales can collaborate without toggling between disconnected apps. If ease-of-use and built-in automation are priorities, HubSpot rarely disappoints. However, businesses need to weigh two significant limitations. First, HubSpot's cost can escalate quickly as contact volumes, features, or users grow. Marketing automation and sales modules are bundled separately, and enabling advanced functions (custom reporting, hierarchical teams, A/B testing) often means jumping to higher-priced tiers. Companies managing rapid expansion or with large sales rosters may see monthly costs balloon, outpacing expectations set during an initial free trial. Second, customization options beyond HubSpot’s standard modules are relatively constrained. While workflows and dashboards can be tailored, highly specific business processes, or nonstandard data structures, are harder to implement, and deeper customization may require external developers or costly add-ons. Choose HubSpot when your top priorities are rapid deployment, reliability, and comprehensive marketing automation, especially if your processes closely fit the workflows the platform provides out-of-the-box. If you need intensive custom development or complete control over your CRM infrastructure, or if budget predictability during scaling is crucial, you’ll want to weigh these limitations carefully. For additional insight on HubSpot’s landscape, see Best HubSpot Alternatives 2026: Tools for Every CRM Need . For enterprise-scale and deep integrations: Salesforce CRM Salesforce CRM stands out as the dominant CRM choice for enterprises needing comprehensive capabilities, deep customization, and smooth integration with a vast ecosystem of business applications. It consistently outperforms Zoho CRM in the scope of features, automation options, and scalability for global organizations. But the breadth comes with steeper costs and steeper learning curves, making Salesforce excessive for most small or mid-sized businesses focused on value and agility. Salesforce offers one of the most extensive marketplaces, supporting thousands of third-party integrations. Everything from marketing automation and e-commerce to advanced analytics and support tools. Teams working across multiple business units or geographies rely on this flexibility. Its platform provides customization at nearly every layer: users can develop custom objects, workflows, and page layouts, or build entirely bespoke apps within the CRM environment. While this allows precise alignment with unique business processes, it also raises the complexity of deployment and ongoing management. Compared to Zoho CRM, which targets a low-cost, all-in-one model suitable for SMBs, Salesforce licensing is significantly more expensive, often requiring both per-user fees and additional costs for advanced features or integrations. Many organizations also turn to certified Salesforce consulting partners for onboarding and integration work. An added cost and resource commitment that’s rarely necessary with simpler platforms like Zoho or HubSpot . Where Salesforce excels is in handling sophisticated, multi-department data flows and governance, making it the platform of record for Fortune 500s, regulated industries, and companies with complex reporting needs. However, for businesses mainly seeking to streamline their sales pipeline or replace Zoho CRM’s basic automation, the investment in Salesforce can quickly become overkill. Teams with moderate requirements may find themselves paying for feature depth and configurability they’ll never use. For buyers weighing this choice, it's critical to consider both direct costs and the hidden operational demands. Salesforce’s flexibility is unmatched for organizations with dedicated IT resources and a need for deep process alignment, but SMBs and cost-focused teams will often be better served by simpler (and far less expensive) platforms. See our Best Salesforce Alternatives for 2026 guide for more scenario-specific recommendations. For sales-focused execution: Pipedrive Pipedrive is a sales-first CRM designed for teams that want clear, visual pipeline management and a clutter-free experience. It excels at helping sales reps track deals, move leads through simple stages, and focus directly on closing. Without the overhead of marketing or project tools. For businesses where sales execution is the top priority and administrative friction is a constant annoyance, Pipedrive is a strong contender. Pipedrive’s core appeal lies in its streamlined pipeline design and user-friendly interface. Every function centers on the idea of helping teams see their sales progress at a glance. Pricing is transparent and competitive, making it accessible for startups and growth-focused teams. Unlike feature-heavy suites that can overwhelm, Pipedrive’s simplicity ensures a shallow learning curve and quick onboarding. However, these design choices bring real tradeoffs. Pipedrive’s focus on pipeline management means advanced customization, marketing automation, and workflow flexibility are limited compared to more comprehensive CRMs. Teams looking to build out detailed reporting, automate complex business processes, or collaborate beyond straightforward sales will quickly reach its limits. This makes it best suited for organizations where the sales pipeline is king, but not for those scaling into cross-departmental complexity. For teams trying to escape Zoho CRM’s performance hiccups and challenging interface, Pipedrive provides an antidote through clarity and ease of use. But if your needs extend beyond sales, such as integration with broader business operations or deep customization, it may be worth exploring platforms like Salesforce or custom solutions designed for high-complexity workflows. For a focused, effective sales pipeline tool, though, Pipedrive stays in its lane and delivers. Migration: What to expect when switching from Zoho CRM Switching from Zoho CRM to a new platform involves more than just exporting contacts and importing them elsewhere. A smooth migration depends on data prep, integration mapping, careful oversight, and active user transition planning. Key steps include cleaning and reformatting legacy data, ensuring vital information isn’t lost in translation, and managing inevitable integration or workflow mismatches that emerge between the old and new systems. Data export from Zoho CRM often surfaces overlooked issues. Standard exports might leave out custom field values, attachments, or activity history, and some teams miss crucial audit logs or integration-specific metadata. Prior to importing into your new CRM, you’ll need to standardize, deduplicate, and clean data so information matches the structure and requirements of the new platform. Teams frequently underestimate the manual effort required to get datasets migration-ready. Messy or misaligned data during this stage can result in lost leads, misattributed deals, or unusable reports post-move. Integration and workflow mapping present another source of friction. Zoho CRM may have custom functions or automation connecting to tools like email systems, quoting engines, or analytics suites. Replicating those in a new system isn’t always straightforward. Each CRM alternative offers different integration options, so your team should catalog mission-critical automations and plan for either equivalent replacements or workarounds. Failing to do this upfront risks disconnected systems or inefficient patchwork solutions. Change management is critical for successful adoption. Even a technically perfect migration can falter if users aren’t comfortable with the new CRM’s navigation or processes. Establish training early, communicate why workflows may feel different, and gather ongoing feedback. Neglecting user onboarding leads to lost productivity and low engagement with the new tool. Some of the most disruptive pitfalls include missing legacy data, mismatched integrations, and downtime during cutover. To minimize risk, conduct parallel runs, testing the new CRM while the old system remains live, and maintain a complete data backup before final switchover. Which Zoho CRM alternative should you choose? The best Zoho CRM alternative comes down to your company’s size, workflow complexity, budget, and control requirements: budget-conscious sales teams gravitate toward Pipedrive or Monday CRM; marketing-led SMBs typically benefit from HubSpot; process-driven mid-market companies and enterprises find Creatio CRM, Salesforce, or Microsoft Dynamics 365 a better fit for deep customization or integrations; businesses demanding full workflow control and infrastructure independence should evaluate custom solutions like Miniloop. Limitations like per-seat pricing, customization ceilings, and migration complexity vary widely. So defining your must-haves and total cost is essential before switching. Creatio CRM delivers strong no-code customization capabilities, empowering business users to adapt workflows and automations without developer involvement. Off-the-shelf options like Salesforce also provide extensive configurability, but typically require expert administrators or consultants. Businesses needing truly bespoke processes should investigate custom-built or highly extensible platforms over template-driven solutions. How do pricing structures differ among Zoho CRM alternatives? Zoho CRM and most mainstream platforms use tiered, per-user monthly pricing that ramps up cost as teams grow or require more features. Some, like HubSpot, offer free plans with essential features but quickly add charges for advanced modules. Miniloop uses a project-based pricing model without per-seat charges, focusing on an upfront or annual fee covering the custom system and support. Other options may provide modular add-ons or charge for API access, storage, or support levels. Understanding the full pricing stack, including mandatory upgrades or minimum seat counts, is essential to evaluate total cost of ownership. Can I keep my data on my own servers with any alternatives? Most mainstream CRMs are offered as fully-managed cloud services and do not permit on-premise hosting. Miniloop uniquely supports hosting on the client's own infrastructure, granting direct control over data residency and security. This is particularly valuable for organizations with strict compliance requirements or preferences for infrastructure independence. Some enterprise platforms like Salesforce offer industry-specific or private cloud options but generally at higher price points and limited flexibility. Always confirm data portability and hosting options during your evaluation. How steep is the learning curve for switching from Zoho CRM? The transition to a new CRM can range from straightforward to complex depending on the similarity of user interfaces, feature sets, and workflow logic. Solutions with intuitive design and robust onboarding, like HubSpot or Pipedrive, may present a gentler learning curve. More customizable options such as Salesforce or custom-built platforms like Miniloop may require extra time for training as users adapt to new processes or tools. Effective migration planning and user education are critical to reducing disruptions. Aligning the new system to existing workflows helps minimize friction during the switch. What hidden costs should buyers consider when moving away from Zoho? Hidden costs include data migration expenses, potential downtime during transition, and the need for retraining staff on new systems. Some platforms charge for exporting data, accessing advanced features, or additional support during onboarding. Customizations that were included by default in Zoho CRM might require paid add-ons or external consultants on alternative platforms. Be wary of recurring costs not reflected in base pricing, such as storage overruns, API usage, or essential integrations. A thorough cost analysis must factor in both initial migration and long-term operational expenses. Why do companies outgrow Zoho CRM as they scale? As organizations grow, they often encounter limitations in Zoho CRM's ability to adapt to increasingly complex workflows and custom data structures. The reliance on tiered plans and per-user fees can significantly inflate costs at larger scales, making it less viable for teams with advanced requirements. Rigid templates and finite customization options force teams into workarounds or fragmented processes, reducing efficiency. Companies also report challenges with data residency and integration flexibility as technical needs advance. Over time, these factors push growing businesses to seek platforms with true workflow ownership and cost predictability.

body_text: Halfway through the year and it is a good time to consider the housing market and see what is going on. From an investment standpoint, we are following the non-agency residential CMO market for reasons explained below. First things first, let's look at mortgage rates: What is curious is that we are seeing about a 20bps spread from where we are this year compared to last year. That spread with the 10-year treasury yield is about 200bps. Furthermore, between 4/24/2021 and 4/7/2022 there was not a single weekly average 30-year fixed mortgage rate reading above 5.00% according to Freddie Mac's data. The 30Y mortgage crossed the 5% threshold on April 14th, 2022. It had not crossed that 5% line since February 2011. 11 years! That being said, it appears that Americans just waiting to move and sitting on their 3% mortgage is starting to slow down. Active US housing inventory is starting to perk up: But even with an increase in inventory, the housing supply gap remains. So, the question is: who will win? Sellers holding onto low-rate mortgages or buyers waiting out high mortgage rates? The percent of US homes for sale 0.7% of total US housing, nearing the lowest in nearly 5 decades. Existing homeowners are still strong on their mortgage payments but consumer credit in general is showing signs of trouble. Mortgage delinquencies remain near 20-year lows while other credit sector hint at trouble. Especially with credit card delinquencies and student loan payments. We won't do a deep dive into the homebuilder economy here today. However, homebuilder incentive rates are worth investigating. Typically, sales incentives are somewhere between 4-6% of sale price. In Q2 2026, PulteHomes rates rose to 10.4%. The 15 largest publicly traded homebuilders saw gross margin compression between Q1 2025 and Q1 2026. From an investment standpoint, we really like the non-agency residential CMO market. The underlying value characteristics are a result of the market crisis, market technicals, and the resilient housing market of the last 15+ years. The seasoning is an important characteristic. The surviving subprime borrowers of 2003-2005 and 2006-2007 are much different than subprime borrowers today. Stable prepayment speeds, declining default rates, and loss writebacks are all characteristics of the subprime market. And you can really see and understand this aspect through mortgage amortization. Homeowner equity can increase from either rising home prices or decreasing mortgage loan balances. You can see de-leveraging around 7% each year as a result. The housing market is in a bit of flux and it looks as if "higher" rates will be the norm for the foreseeable future. Putting the 30-year mortgage rate back to historic norms. As an investor, there might be some interesting pockets to take advantage of as a result of the 2008 GFC.
